title: How to Interpret the Parables of Jesus
subtitle: A guide to interpreting the parables of Jesus, finding the one main point, reading them in light of the kingdom of God, and recovering their original sting

sections.title: Stories With Teeth
sections.body:
We have domesticated the parables. We hand them to children with felt boards and friendly animals and a tidy moral at the end, and we forget that grown men picked up rocks after some of them.

The parables were not safe. They were weapons.

Jesus told them to a hostile crowd, to religious leaders who wanted him dead, to disciples who kept missing the point. They were designed to slip past a listener's defenses, to get him nodding along to a story before he realized the story was about him, and then to spring the trap. A parable is a short story that hides a sharp edge inside an ordinary picture. To read one well is to feel that edge again, the way the first crowd felt it, before the centuries wrapped it in flannel and sentiment. The moment a parable stops making you uncomfortable, you can be fairly sure you have misread it.

sections.title: Look for One Main Point, Not a Code
sections.body:
The oldest mistake with parables is allegory: treating every detail as a secret symbol to be decoded. The road is human stubbornness, the inn is the church, the two coins are the two sacraments, and so on, until the story disappears under the interpreter's cleverness.

This is not how a parable works. A parable is built to make one main point, or at most one point per main character, and the details are mostly there to make the story run, not to carry hidden meanings.

There is one important caution. A few parables Jesus himself interpreted with some detail, like the sower, and there we follow his lead. But the rule for the rest holds firm. Ask what single truth this story was built to drive home, and resist the urge to find a meaning behind every shrub and coin. The parable of the prodigal son is not a treasure hunt of symbols. It is one devastating picture of a father's love and an elder brother's cold heart. Find the point. Let the details serve it. Do not bury the story under your ingenuity.

sections.title: Almost All of Them Are About the Kingdom
sections.body:
Ask what the parables are mostly about and the Gospels answer plainly. They are about the kingdom of God. The kingdom is like a mustard seed, like leaven, like a treasure in a field, like a man who sowed good seed. Over and over, Jesus is doing one thing: showing what it looks like when God's reign breaks into the world through him.

This is the frame that keeps interpretation honest. Before you ask what a parable means for your finances or your friendships, ask what it reveals about the kingdom and the King.

The kingdom in these stories is often hidden, small, easy to despise at the start, and then suddenly overwhelming. It demands everything and is worth more than everything. It divides people, not by their resumes but by their response to the King who stands in front of them telling the story. Read the parables as windows into that kingdom, and they snap into focus. Read them as standalone life lessons, and you will get advice where Jesus was offering a reign.

sections.title: Recovering the Original Sting
sections.body:
The hardest and most important work is to recover what the parable did to its first audience. These stories landed in a specific room, on specific people, and they were aimed.

Find the target. Who was Jesus talking to, and what did this story do to them.

The parable of the good Samaritan is not a gentle nudge to be kind. It was told to a lawyer trying to justify himself, and it made the hated half breed enemy the hero and the religious professionals the men who walked past, which would have stung a Jewish audience like a slap. The parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector was aimed straight at people confident in their own righteousness, and it sent the wrong man home justified. To interpret a parable, you have to identify who it was meant to wound, and then ask the question that finishes the job. Am I in this story. Am I the one who walked past. Am I the elder brother standing outside the party, refusing to go in.

sections.title: Until It Turns and Looks at You
sections.body:
Here is where parable interpretation becomes more than a method. The right reading does not end with information. It ends with exposure.

David heard a parable from Nathan about a rich man who stole a poor man's lamb, and he burned with anger and demanded the man's life, and Nathan said four words that ended David's hiding: you are the man. That is what a parable is for. It gets you to pass judgment on the man in the story before you realize you have passed it on yourself.

So the last move in interpreting any parable is to let it turn and look at you. Not the people who first heard it. You. The point of finding the original sting is to feel it land in your own century, on your own self righteousness, on your own cold elder brother heart. A parable you can teach without flinching is a parable you have not finished reading. Let it do to you what it did to David. Then you will have understood it.
